title: Cut a cable tie off a cable bundle without nicking the cables: hold the bundle, snip the strap beside the tie's head
instruction: Cut the cable tie off the cable bundle without nicking the cables. With one hand, press the bundle down on its left wooden block so that it cannot roll. With the other, take the flush cutters from the tray by their red handles and snip the tie's strap right beside its head: anywhere else the strap lies tight on the insulation, and the jaws would nick a cable. Then put the cutters back in the tray, let go of the bundle and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Technicians cut cable ties off wiring looms, harnesses and network bundles every day. A careless snip nicks the insulation, which can later short or shock someone. The safe way is to hold the bundle still and cut the strap right beside the tie's head, where it stands off the cables.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. Two beech blocks (6 x 5 cm, 5 cm tall) stand 30 cm forward, one 12 cm left and one 16 cm right of the centre line. Across them lies a bundle of seven PVC-insulated copper cables (7 mm each, coloured; 2.1 cm across, 38 cm long, 120 g), running left to right. A black nylon cable tie (4 mm wide strap) is round the bundle 4 cm right of the centre line, between the blocks, its head (7 x 6 x 6 mm) on the near side of the bundle, 30 degrees up from level. A grey ABS tray (18 x 10 cm, 2.5 cm walls) lies 16 cm forward and 25 cm right of the centre line, with two dark rubber rests across it. On the rests lie flush cutters with steel jaws and red PVC-sleeved handles, their jaws pointing forward. The cutters are two steel halves on a pivot (60 g each, 13.4 cm long); the handles are 2.9 cm apart where a hand holds them, 5 cm behind the pivot (about 3.5 cm above the table), and a spring holds the jaws 8 mm open at the tips. Squeezing the handles together closes the jaws; closed 10 degrees, they cut whatever is between the tips. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. 0.0 if the cutters' jaws ever closed on the tie's strap more than 12 mm (along the strap) from the middle of its head, where the strap lies tight on the insulation (a nicked cable). The tie is cut when the jaws close (10 degrees) with their tips within 4 mm of the strap. Otherwise 1.0: the tie cut beside its head, both halves of the cutters back on the tray's rests (within 3 cm of where they lay), the bundle still across its blocks (its middle within 2.5 cm of its line and not below the blocks' tops), each gripper's fingertip centre (TCP) at least 4 cm from the cutters' handles and from the bundle above its left block, and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm of its start); 0.5: the tie cut beside its head; 0.25: the cutters lifted 2 cm out of the tray at some point; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the cutters and the bundle still.
reset_notes: Put a new tie round the bundle at the same place, its head on the near side, lay the bundle back across the blocks and the cutters back in the tray.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the bundle is one rigid body and the tie is glued to it; cutting is a rule: when the jaws close with their tips at the strap, the task file swaps the closed tie for an open one that falls off. A nick is judged by where along the strap the jaws closed, not simulated. The cutters are two rigid halves on a sprung hinge. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
